$$

$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm3\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 3]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/6feea8db62000e44334251a96c39bd8d0d8d7b1ec9a61380f3a5b4b613ea6c80.png)
sketch the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.
e-21657.worked_solution:

For example, when $c_1=1$ and $c_2=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/df8e7ae5f7ff7281cbdbf5849dc94faf59d2421621dc5009b21eeb947485d153.png)

e-21658.knowledge_point: Identifying the Parameters of a System Given Its Phase Portrait
e-21658.problem:
The phase portrait for a system of linear differential equations whose matrix has two complex eigenvalues $\lambda = a \pm b\text{i}$ is shown above. Provide an interpretation of the portrait and determine the possible values of $a.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/6d13d0dfadac45d40b74cb7e740a880305098f0939e2f45d74706c4022183c54.png)
e-21658.worked_solution:
Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},$ where $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = a + b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is unbounded, representing a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise. Thus, we must have $a \neq 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward the origin.

Hence, to insure that $e^{at} \to 0,$ we require $a < 0.$

e-21659.worked_solution:
Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},$ where $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = a + b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a = \text{Re}(\lambda) = 0$ and $e^{at} = e^{0\cdot t} = 1$ for all $t.$ Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin. 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda) = 0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is a center.

$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-1}} \\ y={{field-2}}\end{aligned}

observation.name: Question 1
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2\pm 5\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1,2}=[\pm \text{i},1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-1}} \\ y={{field-2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2\pm 5\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1,2}=[\pm \text{i},1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

observation.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ y={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.52$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.52$ | $0.53$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/2b273edc4f977f2bee4d9a8c41128d4f2071ec39b0840610cbb7ee44492aae3e.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1,$ $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1,$ and ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, the curve $\text{converges}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we have $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

Again, since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/c001f8a99c09e3d1da8c6107a298989c03e64ec58c23319ce0837a757c5ddafd.png)

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ y={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.52$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.52$ | $0.53$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/2b273edc4f977f2bee4d9a8c41128d4f2071ec39b0840610cbb7ee44492aae3e.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1,$ $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1,$ and ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, the curve $\text{converges}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we have $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

Again, since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/c001f8a99c09e3d1da8c6107a298989c03e64ec58c23319ce0837a757c5ddafd.png)

observation.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $-0.71$ | $-1$ |
| $y$ | $5$ | $3.54$ | $0$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/9446137440c19f9aca73c9c666089ecff5a7712ee3f389ab891a150c13ffa780.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1$ and $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1.$ Thus, the obtained curve is $\text{bounded}.$ So, we have $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $-0.71$ | $-1$ |
| $y$ | $5$ | $3.54$ | $0$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/9446137440c19f9aca73c9c666089ecff5a7712ee3f389ab891a150c13ffa780.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1$ and $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1.$ Thus, the obtained curve is $\text{bounded}.$ So, we have $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=25x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 5\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1,2}=[\pm \text{i},5]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={{field-1}} \\ y={{field-2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{20}$ | $\frac{\pi }{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $-0.71$ | $-1$ |
| $y$ | $5$ | $3.54$ | $0$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/9446137440c19f9aca73c9c666089ecff5a7712ee3f389ab891a150c13ffa780.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)|\le 1$ and $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)|\le 1.$ Thus, the obtained curve is $\text{bounded}.$ So, we have $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069757/assets/0678458809cf39967d7dda0d1ffbe4d43541ec309266bd08da6245ec23f6439d.png)

before.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to 0,$ we require $a<0.$

observation.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to 0,$ we require $a<0.$

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to 0,$ we require $a<0.$

{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to \infty ,$ we require $a>0.$

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to \infty ,$ we require $a>0.$

decision.explanation: Both eigenvalues ±4i have real part zero. Nonzero trajectories are closed ellipses (4x²+y² is conserved), so the origin is a center.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=8x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$
Since 
{{field-1}},
the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{0\cdot t}=1$ for all $t.$ Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin. 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )=0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a center}.$

Let v=p+qi, where p,q∈R2, be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=a+bi.

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by xcomplex(t)=veλt.

Using Euler's formula, we obtain xcomplex(t)=ve(a+bi)t=eat(cos⁡(bt)+isin⁡(bt))(p+qi)=eat(cos⁡(bt)p−sin⁡(bt)q)+ieat(sin⁡(bt)p+cos⁡(bt)q).

Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1eat(cos⁡(bt)p−sin⁡(bt)q)+c2eat(sin⁡(bt)p+cos⁡(bt)q), where the parts (cos⁡(bt)p−sin⁡(bt)q) and (sin⁡(bt)p+cos⁡(bt)q) are bounded.

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{0\cdot t}=1$ for all $t.$ Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin. 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )=0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a center}.$

after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda =-1\pm 3\text{i}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$
Since 
{{field-1}},
the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=-1<0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )<0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable spiral (sink)}.$

Let v=p+qi, where p,q∈R2, be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=a+bi.

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda =-1\pm 3\text{i}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$
Since

the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=-1<0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )<0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable spiral (sink)}.$

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{0\cdot t}=1$ for all $t.$ Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin. 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )=0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a center}.$

decision.explanation: Both eigenvalues have real part −2<0 and nonzero imaginary parts. Solutions spiral toward the origin with exponential decay e^{-2t}, making it a stable spiral (sink).

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)-2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda =-2\pm 5\text{i}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$
Since 
{{field-1}},
the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=-2<0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )<0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable spiral (sink)}.$

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=-2<0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward the origin as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )<0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable spiral (sink)}.$

decision.explanation: Both eigenvalues have real part 4>0 and nonzero imaginary parts. Solutions rotate while growing exponentially as e^{4t}, so the origin is an unstable spiral (source).

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t)-7y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7x(t)+4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda =4\pm 7\text{i}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$
Since 
{{field-1}},
the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=4>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )>0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable spiral (source)}.$

content.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=4>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )>0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable spiral (source)}.$
